newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean opposition demands restart of Hanbo probe.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean opposition demands restart of Hanbo probe.

text.p: South Korea's main opposition on Thursday demanded a new probe into a loan scandal involving the failed Hanbo Steel Co, lashing out at state prosecutors for what it called a "disappointing" investigation.
Separately, the prosecutors said they had asked President Kim Young-sam's son to appear at their office on Friday for questioning in connection with the scandal.

The prosecutors will question Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, over his libel complaint against six opposition politicians who accused him of peddling influence in giving massive loans to Hanbo, a prosecution official said.
Kim Hyun-chul has said he had nothing to do with five trillion won ($5.8 billion) worth of loans that Hanbo Steel racked up before being declared insolvent on January 23.
He filed the libel complaint on Tuesday.
Shin Nak-yun, vice-president of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics, told parliament that her party would ask independent prosecutors to restart the scandal.
"The prosecution's announcement totally ignored the people's aspiration," Shin said. "We can't help but rely on the people's power to uncover the truth."

State prosecutors, announcing the outcome of a probe that has lasted almost a month, on Wednesday indicted 10 people, including a former cabinet minister and three ruling party legislators, on charges of bribery and embezzlement in the loans for kickback scandal.
Shin said her party would seek a televised hearing during a separate parliamentary probe, for which a special committee had already been formed in the National Assembly.

She did not say if her party had sought to begin yet another investigation by independent prosecutors, but a National Congress official said the party would seek legislation to allow them to restart the probe.
The official said the party wanted a court to appoint respected lawyers as independent prosecutors for the new investigation.

Senior prosecutor Choi Byung-koog said the prosecution had run into problems because key evidence had been destroyed, including Hanbo's account books before 1993. Cash bribes were extremely difficult to track down, he added.

The prosecution is relying heavily on testimony by Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo, one of those indicted along with former company treasurer Kim Jong-kook. Hanbo Steel is the flagship of South Korea's 14th-biggest congolomerate.

Leading local newspapers and radio commentators also accused the prosecution of failing to reveal what they called the real powers who pressured banks into offering loans to financially shaky Hanbo Steel.

In an editorial, the Chosun Ilbo daily said prosecutors "plucked only a few feathers and ignored the body" although President Kim himself called the Hanbo scandal a "typical example" of corruption still widespread in South Korea".
"This investigation is a complete failure," Chosun Ilbo said. "There is not a single Korean who believes the outcome of the prosecution probe is the truth behind the Hanbo incident."
The Hanbo scandal has badly damaged the political credibility of President Kim who has tried to project an image as an anti-graft crusader since he took office in 1993.
"Is this the rooting out of corruption?" Shin said of the prosecution probe into Hanbo. "Has the Kim Young-sam government abandoned his promise four years after he took office?"

Among those indicted were members of the president's inner circle that backed his rise to power. They are former home affairs minister Kim Woo-suk, who quit last week before he was charged with bribery, and legislators Hong In-gil and Hwang Byung-tai.
